summary: This work shows that a permanent electric dipole on a qubit can suppress cavity-mediated Purcell decay by displacing oscillator wave functions and reducing transverse qubit–cavity exchange, while preserving longitudinal readout coupling. In the displaced rotating-wave approximation, the exchange vanishes exactly at $\eta = \sqrt{2}$; in the full-transverse model, strong suppression persists at $\eta_{\mathrm{FT}} = 2.60$, yielding cavity-mediated lifetime improvements from $\kappa T_1 = 11.1$ to $47.3$ and single-shot readout error reduction from $0.21$ to $0.07$ at fixed pointer separation.
motivation: Readout and control of superconducting qubits in cavities relies on transverse coupling that inevitably opens a Purcell decay channel. This work explores whether a built-in static asymmetry—a permanent dipole—can internally suppress this cavity-mediated loss without external Purcell filters, leveraging Franck–Condon overlap zeros analogous to those in molecular transport.
method: The authors model a two-level qubit with transverse coupling $g_x$ and permanent-dipole longitudinal coupling $g_p$ to a cavity. They analytically derive Franck–Condon factors $F_n(\eta)$ (where $\eta = g_p/\omega_c$) for the transverse matrix element, identify the displaced-RWA exchange zero at $\eta_0 = \sqrt{2}$, and compute dressed open-system decay rates in the full-transverse Hamiltonian including counter-rotating terms, benchmarking against a longitudinal readout protocol with fixed pointer separation.
result: At $\eta_{\mathrm{FT}} = 2.60$ in the full-transverse model with $g_x/\omega_c = 0.030$, $\Delta/\omega_c = 0.10$, and $\kappa/\omega_c = 10^{-3}$, the cavity-mediated decay rate is suppressed close to the non-cavity floor ($\gamma_{1,\mathrm{floor}}/\omega_c = 2 \times 10^{-5}$), increasing $\kappa T_1$ from $11.1$ to $47.3$ and reducing estimated single-shot readout error from $0.207$ to $0.071$ at matched steady-state pointer separation $|\Delta \alpha_{ss}| = 2$ with detection efficiency $\eta_{\mathrm{det}} = 0.40$.
